Can 22nm ReRAM Replace
DDR5 in a Commodity DIMM?

Evaluation of 22nm Memristor-Based Main Memory (MBMM) in Commodity DIMM Architectures

This deck follows the short project book: four ReRAM tracks and a JEDEC-sourced DDR5-4800 baseline through one cross-layer pipeline, at one matched array organization, on six workload traces.

Yuval Kogan · For Prof. Shahar Kvatinsky · September 2026

Short project book; the complete technical report and knowledge base is a separate document.

SayOne sentence of framing: this is the short book's argument in 27 slides, and every number on every slide is a number the book carries. Book title page and Section 1.3.
The question2 / 27

Why This Question, Now

  • Economic pressure. By late 2025 the reallocation of DRAM wafers to High-Bandwidth Memory for AI accelerators had opened a severe supply-demand gap for ordinary DIMM memory [1], [2]
  • Physical pressure. DRAM's planar cell is held back by capacitor leakage and short-channel effects, and commodity DDR5 is fabricated at the end of the capacitor's scaling roadmap [3]. A resistive cell stores state as resistance, so it has no capacitor to scale and needs no refresh
  • The question is narrow and practical: can memristor-based non-volatile memory substitute for DRAM in a standard DIMM?
  • One constraint shapes every answer to it: writes physically wear the cell, so endurance is finite, and any viable DRAM replacement has to buy its lifetime architecturally rather than from the device
  • The claim of this work is a balanced verdict, not an advocacy case
SayTwo pressures, one narrow question, one binding constraint. Say the last bullet out loud: the deliverable is a verdict with its caveats attached, not a case for ReRAM. Book Sections 1.1 and 1.3.

mbmm_master.py orchestrates the whole sequence as one gated flow: no result is accepted that did not come through it. It takes the replay window in nanoseconds and converts it to each technology's own cycle budget, so every configuration replays the same wall-clock window.

The results come from frozen datasets, not a live working directory: a 120-run primary matrix of twenty configurations against six workloads, seven sensitivity series that each change one flag, a 1024-organization axis and a one-channel control run, every one carrying a manifest of its flags and provenance columns on every processed row. The Python layer carries 783 tests at this revision's closing verification, plus a regression harness against a stored reference.

SayNVSim characterizes exactly one chip; everything downstream is NVMain replicating that chip and wrapping it in its own controller. The gate sentence is the one to say plainly: a pipeline change is not considered to have worked until the suite, the harness and mbmm_master.py all pass. Book Section 2.1, Figure 1.

NVSim has no multi-level-cell model, so the MLC rows apply an analytic penalty on the SLC characterization: 1.5x read latency, 3.263x write latency, twice the capacity behind the same chips, both multipliers derived by the same bandwidth-ratio method from the EMBER macro's own published measurements [11], [12]. Leakage and die area are unchanged, because the array is the same array.

SayThis is the single most consequential methodological choice in the evaluation: one matched organization, so every cross-technology difference is a device difference. Book Table 1 and Section 2.2.

Baselines and Traces

  • DDR5-4800, 16 GiB RDIMM, eight 16 Gb x8 devices, two independent 32-bit subchannels serving 64 B as a 16-beat burst. Timings from JESD79-5 [20]: 40-39-39, CWL 38, tWR 30 ns, tRRD_S 8, tFAW 32, tREFI 3.906 us with tRFC 295 ns. Its power model is calibrated to vendor IDD tables, which are specification limits rather than typicals, so it is a worst-case-current baseline reported as a band
  • PCM (legacy) [21] as the floor-power reference: constants inherited unmodified from NVMain's bundled example, never run through NVSim, no access-device topology stated
  • Published silicon, 1T1R SILICON and 1S1R SILICON, generated from the datasheets of [13] and [14] and run on the same traces and module geometry: the counterweight to every projected media latency
  • 64 bytes for every technology; the ReRAM interface is an assumed 800 MHz with no independent ReRAM citation, quantified by the clock sweep on slide 9

Lessons6 / 27

What the Pipeline Taught Me (1 to 4)

  • 1. Match the array organization before you compare cells. NVSim charges memristor cells no leakage at all, so a chip's leakage is peripheral circuitry and follows mat count. Two different column muxes meant two different mat counts, and what I was reading as a property of the access device was a property of my own configuration
  • 2. Establish the time base and the window before you read any rate. A rate is a count divided by a time, and if the time is unestablished the rate is decoration. Fix the unit first, and reconcile the trace against the generator's own counters
  • 3. The classic latency metric can lie under saturation. A short queue reports a fast average over the few requests it admits while the rest of the burst backs up outside the controller, where the total-latency counter cannot see it. Both numbers belong in the same table
  • 4. A configuration template inherits more than it declares. Raising a clock does not rescale the cycle counts that came with the template, and nothing in the simulator objects. A cycle count is not a time
SayThese are stated as mechanisms on purpose: a mechanism transfers to the next project and a retired value does not. Book Chapter 3.
Lessons7 / 27

What the Pipeline Taught Me (5 to 8)

  • 5. Read a simulator's power accounting to the line. A background-power path divided a rank's power by its device count and never multiplied it back, so a per-device figure wore a module label. No warning, no anomaly, a plausible number
  • 6. Charge a device latency exactly once. The repair was a rule and a check rather than a constant: tRCD plus tCAS must sum to the device read latency rounded up to whole interface cycles, and the generator re-reads the rendered configuration to confirm it
  • 7. Keep a silicon counterweight beside every projection. A circuit-level model will happily project a nanosecond array, and no fabricated ReRAM part reads or writes in nanoseconds. A projection without a fabricated reference beside it is an argument about a model, not about a technology
  • 8. Know which timing key sits on the request path. In the default configuration the cell write time sits in write recovery and reaches the request path only when a write closes its row, where it is charged to the subarray's next activation; a write into an already open row charges nothing beyond the burst and the turnaround, and neither branch delays the write's own completion
SayLesson 8 is the one that sets up the bracket slide: which key holds the number decides whether a write penalty reaches the results at all. Book Chapter 3, lessons 5 to 8.

The Interface Clock Is Three Quarters of the Number

  • Of the 41.40 ns 1T1R SLC average under GCC, 11.25 ns is NVSim device time, charged once as tRCD plus tCAS; the other 30.2 ns is NVMain's protocol cycle counts at the assumed 800 MHz interface

  • The magnitude is model-dependent: 41.4 against 83.1 ns is the outcome of one clock choice, not a device ratio

MLC and the Write-Pulse Bracket

Average total latency (ns), full DIMMGCC, defaultGCC, boundingOFMAP, defaultOFMAP, bounding
1T1R SLC41.448.3353.1696.6
1T1R MLC44.565.8512.01,649.9

1S1R MLC37.972.4652.92,498.7

The primary matrix was re-run with the mapping inverted: the same latency written to the write pulse, write recovery held at one cycle, so every write's completion carries the pulse. Against DDR5's 234.3 ns on the output map each ratio becomes a bracket: 1.507x to 2.973x for 1T1R SLC, 1.671x to 3.912x for 1S1R SLC, 2.185x to 7.042x for 1T1R MLC and 2.787x to 10.665x for 1S1R MLC. These are media latencies at an assumed 800 MHz interface, not device latencies of any shipped part.

What produced the bracket is not the same thing on the CPU traces as on the write burst. On GCC, LBM and STREAM the rise equals the write fraction times the cell pulse to within 1%, because the row-buffer hit share is about 0.03% and nearly every write closed its row. On the output map 76% of accesses hit an open row and the rise is 21 to 23 times the per-write pulse, so it is mostly subarray blocking that the default mode never charged. The bracket is an upper end of the write-path cost inside this model, not a prediction of a device, and a reader who takes the output-map figure as the cell pulse added to every write will be wrong by a factor of about 22. "Below DDR5 on the CPU traces" survives at the upper end for all four projected tracks, the worst case being 1S1R MLC under GCC at 72.398 against 83.111 ns, 0.871x of DDR5; and no endurance number moves.

One comparison bounds the whole MLC treatment: published program-and-verify data reports an average of 49 pulses per level move, median 36 [28], and the closest published two-bit array result is MLC phase-change memory at more than seventy iterations for a 9.7 us total write [29], so the 3.263x multiplier understates the media-level MLC write cost by one to two orders of magnitude. TLC and QLC carry no defensible number, only a qualitative trend.

The projection caveat, all three parts. First, every ReRAM latency here is a media number at NVSim-projected device timings, an array-core projection rather than a measurement of a fabricated part. Second, the same DIMM built from published silicon timings averages 11.9 us and 379 us under GCC and does not finish the LBM window, completing 18.2% and 1.0% of it. Third, on the write-dominated AlexNet output-map burst the projected DIMM is slower than DDR5, 353.1 ns for 1T1R SLC and 391.5 ns for 1S1R SLC against 234.3 ns.

SayThe bracket answers "how much of the MLC result is a modeling choice" with a measurement instead of an assertion, and the answer is: most of it on the write burst, almost none of it on the CPU traces. Book Section 4.1, the write-pulse bracket table.
Results · Power12 / 27

Where the Watts Are

There is no transistor-versus-selector leakage gap. At the matched organization NVSim assigns both cell types the same 108.384 mW of peripheral leakage per 1 Gb chip, and all four ReRAM full-DIMM configurations sit on one shared static floor of 6.937 W.

Dynamic power is 2.9 to 4.9 mW module-wide under GCC and rises only to 346 to 417 mW under the AI read bursts, under 6% of the total. ReRAM power is leakage, and at the matched organization that is a statement about both cell types equally. The chart is a module-level view; the per-gigabyte normalization, which is the only form in which these modules are comparable, is on the next slide.

SayAttacking that floor is a circuit problem in the sense amplifiers and decoders, not a choice between access devices. Book Section 4.2 and Figure 3.

Results · Power14 / 27

Overhead, Organization and the Selector

  • Fixed per-module overhead moves the arithmetic against ReRAM. 8 GiB of ReRAM carries the same register, power-management IC and PHY overhead as 16 GiB of DDR5, so the required gating fraction rises with it: 94.3% at zero, 97.9% at 0.5 W per module, and beyond 0.79 W parity is out of reach at any gating fraction. The same overhead compresses the ungated ratio, and the parity claim rests on the gated comparison
  • The leakage figure is an organization result, not a cell result. At a 1024 x 1024 organization both cells leak about twice as much, 224.138 and 220.224 mW per chip, still within 2% of each other. Whatever organization is matched, the two cells land together, because chip leakage is peripheral circuitry and follows mat count
  • The selector's sneak current adds nothing to standby power and little during an access. The standby adder is exactly zero at both selector bounds; during an access the budget is 7.56 mW per chip at an ovonic-threshold-switch bound and 0.076 mW at a best-published FAST bound, which at the OTS figure is 0.87% of the module's 6.937 W static floor while a rank is being accessed
  • What binds is tile validity, not leakage. The OTS bound supports a tile of at most 1666 cells a side, so the 2048 x 2048 organization simulated here is not valid at present-day selector quality, while the FAST bound supports 166,666. Every 1S1R number in this work is conditional on a selector better than today's production ovonic threshold switch
SayNVSim models no selector physics at all, so the selector layer is a standalone analytic layer on top of it. The tile-validity result is a real caveat on the density case, not a footnote. Book Section 4.2, results/selector_layer.json.

Endurance: the Projection and the Requirement

The write distribution measured per line location inside the 250 ms window, carried onto a 64 GiB module at the best-sourced 106 cycle rating [31], under four wear-leveling policies. 1T1R SLC, full DIMM, one write per line per request.

WorkloadWrite rateNo levelingRandomized Start-GapIdealRequired endurance (ideal)
GCC0.88 M/s7.7 h7.7 to 15.4 h38.6 yr2.6 x 105
LBM9.54 M/s23.2 h0.20 yr3.6 yr2.8 x 106
STREAM7.99 M/s69.5 h0.96 yr4.3 yr2.3 x 106

Ranges in the randomized Start-Gap column mark cases where the hottest line fails before the gap completes its first rotation. Required endurance is the per-cell cycle count a ten-year life would demand at this write rate and capacity: against the 106 planning value GCC clears the bar fourfold under ideal leveling and everything else fails it by 2.3 to 6.5x, the randomized Start-Gap requirements being 6.3, 6.5 and 4.3 x 106. A ten-year ReRAM main memory needs a cell in the high 106 range and a leveling scheme better than a single-region Start-Gap.

Every row assumes a stationary write distribution: the spatial pattern of writes measured inside the 250 ms window is taken to repeat unchanged for the module's whole life. Every lifetime here is a projection, never a measured lifetime.

SaySay the word projection out loud, every time. The required-endurance column is the same equation solved for endurance rather than for time, which is the form a designer can act on. Book Table 6.
Results · Endurance16 / 27

The Leveling Decides It

  • Viability is decided almost entirely by the wear-leveling mechanism, not by the cell: hours with no leveling against 38.6 years under GCC with ideal leveling, four to five orders of magnitude
  • The traces are sparse: GCC touches 577 row locations, LBM 826 and STREAM 1,954, out of 1,048,576 at the 64 GiB capacity projected here
  • Deterministic Start-Gap [32] recovers essentially nothing over one whole-module region; randomizing the region assignment recovers 0.20 yr under LBM and 0.96 under STREAM, and still nothing under GCC
  • Against intuition, a larger module is worse over a single region: under randomized Start-Gap GCC survives 0.69 years at 8 GiB but only 7.7 hours at 64 GiB

One negative result bounds what the simulation can contribute: it cannot show wear leveling at work. With one whole-module region and one gap move per hundred writes, a 250 ms window makes 2,207 gap moves under GCC and 23,848 under LBM, roughly 10-5 and 10-4 of a rotation, so running the matrix with the remapper off reproduces the primary run's wear statistics and latencies identically. Leveling's effect is carried entirely by the projection, validated against a write-by-write simulator to within 0.3%. Every value is a projection from a distribution measured in a 250 ms window and assumed stationary.

SayIf asked "did you show the leveling working": no, and here is precisely why no feasible window can, and here is what carries the claim instead. Book Section 4.3 and Figure 4.

Results · Sensitivities18 / 27

Queue Depth, and Four Sensitivities

  • Across depths of 8, 32 and 128 the CPU traces do not move at all. Under the AlexNet output-map write burst the two latency measures move in opposite directions: for 1T1R SLC the in-controller average goes 124.9, 353.1, 1,049.2 ns while the end-to-end average goes 680.1, 486.1, 432.5 us
  • That answers the write-queue sizing question: on a write burst a deeper queue pays off end to end, and the in-controller average reports that gain as a regression
  • Organization 1024 x 1024: the 1T1R SLC full DIMM is 4 to 10% faster and every track pays 14.1 to 14.7 W against 6.9 W, the two cells still leaking within 2% of each other
  • A 64 B DDR5 cross-check on a legacy single-channel shape averages 79.6 against 83.1 ns under GCC but holds tCCD below the JEDEC floor, so its advantage is optimistic
  • A plus or minus 20% ReadVoltage sweep moves the power-delay product by less than 4% with read latency invariant, on a pre-revision dataset not comparable with the tables above
  • Every ReRAM figure on this slide is a media latency at the assumed 800 MHz interface, under the same projection caveat as the tables above
SayThis is the one experiment that separates the two latency definitions cleanly, and it is the argument for reporting end-to-end latency alongside the classic metric. Book Section 4.4.

Discussion20 / 27

Near and Far Memory: the Window

  • The window real systems accept is narrow, and it is measured. Local DDR5 measures 111 to 114 ns idle on two-socket servers, with platform baselines of 78 and 115 ns in Microsoft's Pond study and 140 to 193 ns to the far socket [33], [34]. Shipped CXL-attached DRAM expanders measure about 214, 239 and 271 ns idle load-to-use for ASIC-based devices and about 394 ns for an FPGA-based one [33], [35]. Every one of those is a device number
  • No blanket threshold survives contact with that data. Pond's workload study finds applications losing measurable performance at latency increases well below the width of that band while most tolerate an increase of that size [34], so acceptability is a per-workload property, not a number. And the few-hundred-nanosecond band belongs to CXL-attached DRAM devices, not to local DRAM
  • This work's two latency lines sit on opposite sides of that window, and neither is inside it. The projected media is 36.8 to 44.5 ns under GCC and 353.1 to 652.9 ns on the write burst, below the entire window with room for a controller and an error-correction stack; the published-silicon counterweights, 11.9 us and 379 us under GCC, are far above it
  • One mechanism decides how such a device would be used. A CXL-attached region surfaces to Linux as a CPU-less NUMA node, with ACPI HMAT supplying latency and bandwidth per initiator-target pair [36], and what the kernel does with that ranking is page placement, not per-request routing: 4 KiB pages on a millisecond-to-second timescale. A far memory can afford to be slower than DRAM; it cannot afford to be slower by a factor page migration cannot amortize
  • The bandwidth half does not hold as stated either: a shipping x8 CXL 2.0 expander is published at up to 36 GB/s [37], at or below a single DDR5-4800 channel's 38.4 GB/s [35], so CXL adds capacity and bandwidth from a slot that otherwise carries no memory at all. That framing is what makes the density dividend the quantity such a slot is bought for
SayKeep the vocabulary strict on this slide: ours are media numbers, Optane's and CXL's are device numbers, and the two are never compared as though they were the same kind of measurement. Book Section 5.2.

The four ReRAM rows share the assumed 800 MHz interface and carry no controller, ECC or PHY; "burst" is the AlexNet output map, and the second figure of each range is the bounding write-pulse run. DDR5 appears twice on purpose: as the modeled media number this work compares against, and as the measured device latency of a real server, about a third higher. No ReRAM row here is a device number, and no device row is a prediction for ReRAM.

The conditional statement is honest in both directions. ReRAM could serve as far memory only if a device built on it, controller, error correction and a DRAM cache in front of it as in Optane's Memory Mode [39], landed in the same few-hundred-nanosecond class as the measured CXL-attached DRAM devices above. No published ReRAM silicon does. What the projected numbers say is which half of the problem is open: at 36.8 to 44.5 ns of media latency with 1.24x to 2.47x DDR5's die-level density on the selector track, the device physics is not the obstacle. The interface, the error-correction stack and the controller are.

Discussion22 / 27

Bit Errors and Error Correction

Neither NVSim nor NVMain models a bit error anywhere in this pipeline, so this is a literature result set, with three categories kept apart throughout: retention errors, endurance errors, and read-disturb errors.

  • Layer one, the raw device rate. For the cross-point track no measured array bit error rate is published at all; the only numeric figure is a channel model of a 1024 x 1024 array with an ideal selector, 4.29 x 10-4 for the best-positioned cell to 7.33 x 10-2 for the worst [40]. The 1T1R track does have measured macros: below 10-7 after 106 cycles with a smart-write algorithm [41], against 10-3 to 10-2 for HfO2 arrays under adverse cycling [42]
  • Layer two, the selector itself. A measured 1S1R selector reports a per-read disturb rate of 10-9 and 109 read-disturb-free cycles [43], and an ovonic-threshold-switch cross-point cell a failure rate of 9% falling to 0.02% after read-endurance optimization [44]. The selector's own contribution is bounded well below the layer-one array rates: the 1S1R disadvantage is tile validity and sneak current, not error rate
  • Layer three, the design point. The standard persistent-memory design point is a raw rate of 2 x 10-4 corrected with BCH(2312,2048,22) at about 27% coding overhead [45]; DRAM's on-die SECDED tolerates about 10-6 raw [46], and the only shipped NVM media has an SSD sibling rated under one uncorrectable sector per 1017 bits [47]
  • A main memory built on published raw ReRAM error rates is possible, but it needs SSD-class rather than DRAM-class correction, at roughly a 27% cost in bits. And plainly: the modeled latencies exclude ECC decode, so every latency here is optimistic by exactly the decode time such a code would add
SayThe stronger claim sometimes made in discussion, that the error rate rules out a memory system altogether, is not supportable against this literature. The selector layer was built independently of it and agrees with it, applying the same 10% minimum read-margin criterion. Book Section 5.3.
Discussion23 / 27

Limits of the Model

  • The 800 MHz interface is assumed. It carries no ReRAM citation, the only datasheet-verified ReRAM chip I/O clocks located run 80 to 160x slower, and roughly three quarters of every ReRAM latency average is protocol cycles at that clock
  • The write path is a bracket, not a model. The cell write time is charged either as write recovery or, in the bounding run, to every write's completion, and neither end models the program-and-verify loop an MLC part actually runs
  • Power is device-only. Both sides count memory devices, with no register clock driver, power-management IC, PHY, termination or ReRAM-side controller, and the ReRAM power-down energy is a no-savings placeholder
  • No ECC decode sits on the read path, and no coding overhead is charged against the density figures
  • Endurance rests on stationarity. Every lifetime extrapolates a write distribution measured inside a 250 ms window to years, and the leveling schemes are modeled analytically rather than simulated end to end
  • Every ReRAM timing is projected. No fabricated part has matched NVSim's array core, which is why the published-silicon counterweight accompanies every latency table
  • There is no CXL, controller or device model anywhere in this work. The previous two slides position the projected media against measured devices; they do not simulate one

Seven limits, all disclosed rather than discovered.

SayBe the one who raises these before anyone in the room does. Book Section 5.4.
Verdict24 / 27

The Verdict

  • What holds is direction. On the CPU traces the projected media is faster than the DDR5-4800 baseline, and that ordering survives at the upper end of the write-pulse bracket; at a matched organization the cross-point clears DDR5's die-level density and the transistor-gated cell never does. Neither magnitude is robust in the way its direction is
  • What is bounded is the power deficit and the write burst. The per-gigabyte penalty counts memory devices only on both sides and is measured against a baseline that realizes its JEDEC power-down credit while ReRAM's is a no-savings placeholder; gating break-even sits inside, not above, the cited idleness band, so the arithmetic brackets parity for that class and cannot price it. The upper end of the output-map bracket is an upper end of the write-path cost inside this model, not a prediction of a device
  • What is projected is every lifetime, and the latency advantage itself. The endurance claim lives in the leveling mechanism, not the cell, and no figure here is a measured lifetime; the same DIMM at published silicon timings runs in microseconds

Selector-gated 22nm SLC ReRAM is a density play with competitive projected latency and a large, honest power deficit per gigabyte, 12.7x to 17.4x as SLC, device for device and as an upper bound; the transistor-gated variant matches it on leakage and loses on area. Write endurance is the binding constraint and the wear leveling, not the cell, decides it.

Neither cell is a drop-in DDR5 replacement at 22nm.

The projection caveat, all three parts. First, every ReRAM latency here is a media number at NVSim-projected device timings, an array-core projection rather than a measurement of a fabricated part. Second, the same DIMM built from published silicon timings averages 11.9 us and 379 us under GCC and does not finish the LBM window, completing 18.2% and 1.0% of it. Third, on the write-dominated AlexNet output-map burst the projected DIMM is slower than DDR5, 353.1 ns for 1T1R SLC and 391.5 ns for 1S1R SLC against 234.3 ns.

SayThree kinds of statement, kept apart: what holds, what is bounded, what is projected. That separation is the discipline of the whole book, and the last line is the conclusion it has carried since the first version. Book Sections 5.1 and 6.
Future work25 / 27

Future Work

  • Native MLC logic with the write pulse and verify on the path. Replace the analytic penalty with native circuit-level characterization of iterative sensing, and put an iteration-count distribution and a verify-read cost on the request path instead of one scalar pulse
  • Faster-PHY interface parity. The clock sweep quantifies what the 800 MHz assumption is worth; what remains open is a defensible ReRAM PHY rather than an assumed one
  • The Optane reference row completed with loaded-latency data. The only shipped NVM main memory is carried at its idle measured latency; no open figure exists for it under load
  • A CXL Type 3 device model with capacity-bound traces. Model the far position directly, driven by traces that are capacity-bound rather than latency-bound, which none of the six here is
  • ECC decode on the read path. Pricing it needs a decoder latency model and a 27% capacity cost against the density figures, and the latency and density verdicts then have to be re-derived together
  • Endurance-aware scheduling. Wear-leveling algorithms at the controller level, simulated end to end rather than modeled analytically
  • Macro-scale 1T1R array limits. Because chip leakage follows mat count, enlarging the 1T1R subarray is the most direct attack available on the peripheral-leakage floor, reporting leakage per gigabyte as the primary metric
  • A workload that would actually use rank depth. A trace with a large address footprint and a sustained arrival rate above one controller's service rate would turn the strongest negative result into a measurement
SayFrame these as the boundary of the claims rather than as a wish list: each one follows directly from something this work could not settle. Book Chapter 6.
